OMIM:612164.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 4 is strongly linked to STXBP1. Research papers show STXBP1 changes often make the protein work less, which fits this condition. There are also patient studies and natural-history projects that may help families learn more, but some links are only suggestive.

steps.text: Research papers show STXBP1 causes Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 4. This is a well-supported link, not just a guess. [E00001]

Research papers show many STXBP1 changes may make the protein work less. One paper says heterozygous loss-of-function changes were found. Another says changes led to haploinsufficiency, which means too little working STXBP1. [M5aa5e603, M6d03ea65, M42d5a943]

Records show STXBP1 this condition has been included in study plans and patient-data projects. These include a natural-history study, a Europe study on trial readiness, and a survey-based study. [T00064, T00068, T00069, T00070, C00020, C00021, C00022]

Some records also suggest this condition may look like other severe brain-and-seizure conditions. But those similarity records are only hypotheses, so they do not prove a shared cause. [E00224, E00226, E00222, E00225]

uncertainties: The study records do not prove which people with this condition were actually included. Several notes say the disease or change should be confirmed in scope. [T00064, T00068, T00069, T00070, T00075, T00076, T00031, T00032, T00001, T00002]
The similarity links are computed guesses, not proven biology. [E00224, E00226, E00222, E00225]
We do not have detailed results for the listed studies here, only that they exist. This means we cannot say whether they helped or not. [T00064, T00068, T00069, T00070, C00020, C00021, C00022]
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the STXBP1 evidence and the listed study records together. They can check whether any study or data project fits your family’s exact change. [E00001, M5aa5e603, M6d03ea65, M42d5a943, T00064, C00020, C00021, C00022]

OMIM:613721.summary_plain: Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 11 is linked to changes in SCN2A. Research papers show this condition often involves changes that make the sodium channel work more, but some lab work also shows mixed or weaker channel effects. Several studies are listed for this condition, and some nearby conditions may help guide future research, but those links are not proven to be the same disease process.

steps.text: Research papers show SCN2A can cause this condition. That is a strong, curated link. [E00026]
One paper says SCN2A gain-of-function changes may drive early-onset disease. This means the sodium channel may work more than normal. [Mfce5014c]

Another lab study found one change with mixed weaker-and-stronger channel effects. The same study also said repeated use made the channel act more weakly. This points to possible change-to-change differences. [M30b5f5fe, Md58c8bdc]

We also found several research studies that include people with SCN2A-related disease. These include an observational study and drug studies, which shows active research in this area. [T00052, T00053, T00054, C00031, C00032, C00033]
Some records link this condition to similar rare conditions, but those links are only hypotheses. They should not be treated as proof of a shared cause. [E00228, E00229, S00001, Y00003]

uncertainties: The records do not show which exact SCN2A changes were found in most people with this condition.
The mixed and weaker channel findings come from lab work, not direct proof in all patients.
The study records say SCN2A is in the title or keywords, but they also ask for scope confirmation.
The nearby-condition links are only suggested similarities, not proven shared mechanisms.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN2A papers and study records together, especially E00026, Mfce5014c, M30b5f5fe, Md58c8bdc, T00052, T00053, and T00054. They can help you see which changes are best matched to this condition. [E00026, Mfce5014c, M30b5f5fe, Md58c8bdc, T00052, T00053, T00054]

OMIM:614558.summary_plain: Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 13 is linked to changes in SCN8A. Research papers show those changes can make the sodium channel work too much. That can raise brain cell firing and help trigger seizures.

steps.text: We found a direct link between SCN8A and this condition. That link is well supported in curated records.
Research papers show SCN8A changes may make the sodium channel work more. One paper says patient-derived changes have gain-of-function effects.
Another paper says a recurring SCN8A change can impair channel inactivation. That is consistent with brain cells firing too easily and seizures.
Records also show this condition is being studied in SCN8A-focused studies. Those include NBI-921352, PRAX-562, and two study records tied to SCN8A-DEE.
There is also a study shared with Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 11. That shared study does not prove the same cause, but it suggests related care research.

uncertainties: Some study records say to confirm the exact disease or change in scope. That means fit for your family may need expert review.
The gain-of-function message is supported by cited papers, but the papers mention different changes and contexts.
Some links, like shared mechanism or phenotype similarity, are only hypotheses. They should not be treated as proven shared biology.
I do not see detailed age, seizure type, or variant-specific guidance for every child in these records.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN8A papers and the study records together. Focus on the cited SCN8A gain-of-function reports and the SCN8A-DEE study records.

OMIM:613720.summary_plain: Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 7 is linked to KCNQ2. Records show KCNQ2 changes can work less or work more. Some studies and patient resources may help families find experts and research contacts.

steps.text: Research papers show KCNQ2 can cause this condition. The strongest direct link is curated and supported.
Some KCNQ2 changes may make the potassium channel work less. That can fit a loss-of-function change.
Other KCNQ2 changes may make the channel work more. Those reports are tied to different symptoms, so they do not cancel each other out.
Records show KCNQ2-focused studies are underway or listed. These include a natural history study, a phenotype and omics study, and the XEN496 study program.
Research papers also show a registry exists for KCNQ2 families. That can be a place to learn about tracking symptoms and research updates.

uncertainties: We do not have a clear rule that says which KCNQ2 changes cause this condition by themselves.
The higher-function and lower-function findings come from different reports, so the best match for a specific child is still uncertain.
The study records say the condition is in scope, but they also ask for confirmation of the exact disease or change.
We do not have outcome results for the listed studies, only that they exist.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the KCNQ2 change against the cited reports and study records, especially the loss-of-function and gain-of-function papers plus the KCNQ2 study listings.

OMIM:612621.summary_plain: Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 5 is linked to changes in SYNGAP1. Research papers show these changes usually make the gene work less, which can lead to this condition.

Several papers say these changes usually make SYNGAP1 work less. That includes loss-of-function changes and SYNGAP1 haploinsufficiency, which means one working copy is not enough.
We also found studies that include people with this condition. These include a natural history study, a survey study, and a pilot treatment study.
There are also research links to patient groups and registries for related SYNGAP1 care and research. These may help families find updates and study contact paths.

OMIM:615473.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 17 is linked to GNAO1. Research papers suggest this condition can involve changes in GNAO1 that alter G protein signaling. Some records also point to patient studies and a natural history study for GNAO1-related care.

steps.text: Research records show GNAO1 causes Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 17. This is the main known link for this condition.
Some animal studies suggest certain GNAO1 changes may make G protein signaling work too much. That includes the G203R and G184S changes.
Another animal study suggests a severe GNAO1 change may act in a dominant negative way. That means the changed gene may block the normal gene from working well.
Research records also list GNAO1-focused studies and a natural history study. These may help families learn how this condition behaves over time.
Records also show related patient groups and studies for nearby rare epilepsies. These are only similarity clues, not proof of the same cause.

uncertainties: The animal studies do not prove the same change acts the same way in people.
The similarity links are hypotheses and do not prove shared disease causes.
Some study records say the disease name should be checked for fit and scope.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

OMIM:607745.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3 is linked to SCN2A. Research papers also suggest some SCN2A changes make the sodium channel work less. That fits a possible loss-of-function pattern in this condition.

steps.text: Research records show SCN2A can cause Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3. That is the clearest link we found. [E00175]
One published study says an SCN2A change, S863F, reduced current density. This suggests a loss-of-function change, meaning the channel may work less well. [M13d4d49b]
There is also a second SCN2A-related seizure condition in the records. That means related seizure types may overlap, but this is not proof of the same cause or treatment response. [E00252,E00026]
The records also list the FamilieSCN2A Foundation as serving people with this condition. That may be a useful support contact. [C00004]

uncertainties: The loss-of-function idea comes from one cited study and one change only. It may not apply to every SCN2A change in this condition.
We did not find a study record named specifically for Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3.
The two trial records in the input are for SCN2A-DEE, not this exact condition. They may not match your group’s needs.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN2A S863F finding and the exact diagnosis match. If useful, also contact the FamilieSCN2A Foundation for patient-facing support. [M13d4d49b,C00004]

We also found a similar seizure condition linked to SCN8A, but that match is only a guess. It does not prove the same cause or same change here.
Support groups are listed for this condition, so families may have a place to ask questions and find community help.

OMIM:121200.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial neonatal, 1 is linked to KCNQ2 changes. Research papers show KCNQ2 changes can make the potassium channel work less. Some studies also suggest different changes can have different effects.

steps.text: Research records show KCNQ2 causes Seizures, benign familial neonatal, 1. This is a well-supported link. [E00187]

Lab studies show some KCNQ2 changes make the potassium channel work less. One study says a stop change lowered channel expression on the cell surface. Another says haploinsufficiency, meaning too little working protein, is a main mechanism in this condition. [M469654af, M05787647]

One lab study suggests different changes at the same spot can act differently. Y284C and Y284D were linked to different clinical pictures, and they had opposite effects in the test system. This suggests change-specific effects, but it is still lab-based evidence. [Md1dba723]
Records also show KCNQ2-focused studies and a patient group resource. These may help families learn about this condition and related research. [C00010, C00042, C00043, C00044, C00009, T00031, T00032]

uncertainties: The records do not tell us which KCNQ2 change your family has.
The study records do not confirm whether each listed study includes this exact condition.
Some findings are lab studies, so they may not match every child.
The similarity record to another epilepsy type is only a hypothesis and not shared-mechanism proof.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the exact KCNQ2 report alongside the cited KCNQ2-focused study and group resources. That can help match your family’s change to the research more carefully. [E00187, C00010, C00042, C00043, C00044, C00009]
